ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning to Utilize External Context in RAG Systems
PROPOSAL: Investigate using a learned weighting scheme for the external context, where the model predicts weights for each retrieved document based on its relevance to the question and the generated response. We will use a variant of the cross-entropy loss for this, using the retrieved documents as the target and the model's predicted weights as the hypothesis.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline that uses a fixed uniform weighting scheme, and ablate the learned weighting by replacing it with a fixed weighting scheme.
COST: 20 GPU-hours, assuming 1000 queries and 10 retrieved documents each.
PREDICTION: The learned weighting scheme should show a significant reduction in hallucination rates and increase in factual accuracy, particularly in tasks where retrieval is crucial. However, there may be cases where the model overfits to the weighting scheme, reducing generalizability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Invariant Attention Dilation for External Context Utilization
PROPOSAL: Design an attention mechanism that dilates the attention weights of the input tokens (any tokens from d, q) by a factor of the learned weights predicted by the model in proposal 1. This will create a sense of "importance" of the external context over the input tokens, forcing the model to utilize external context more effectively. We will implement this using a learned scale factor amplified with a Cat provozu transformer dilation block.
CONTROLS: Compare with the learned weighting scheme from proposal 1, and a baseline that uses a standard non-dilated transformer attention.
COST: 30 GPU-hours, assuming 1000 queries and 10 retrieved documents each.
PREDICTION: This mechanism should improve the model's ability to ground its responses in the external context, leading to a decrease in hallucination rates and an increase in factual accuracy. However, there may be performance degradation if the dilation parameter is not optimized correctly, leading to a loss of fine-grained information.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Invariant Attention Dilation for External Context Utilization
REVISED PROPOSAL: Modify the learned scale factor to be a function of the distance between the external context tokens and the input tokens, based on the structural information of the query. This way, the model is encouraged to utilize context tokens that are closer to the relevant tokens in the query, and less reliant on internal knowledge. We will implement this using a geodesic distance-based attention mechanism within Cat crore transformer blocks.
CONTROLS: Compare with the previous dilation-based approach (minor modification of 2) effectively serving as an outer baseline,  the baseline non-dilated transformer attention and ablate the distance metric by setting it to zero.
COST: 10 GPU-hours, assuming 1000 queries and 10 retrieved documents each.
PREDICTION: This revised mechanism should improve the model's utilization of external context by focusing on the most relevant tokens, potentially leading to fewer hallucinations and more accurate responses. However, there may be cases where the model overemphasizes the distance and ignores relevant tokens that are farther away.

 TITLE: Regularization Term for Internal Knowledge Utilization
 PROPOSAL: Introduce a regularization term to discourage excessive use of internal knowledge by the model. This can be achieved by adding a penalty term to the loss function that measures the KL-divergence between the model's internal knowledge distribution (e.g., predicted entity representations) and a fixed prior distribution that represents "correct" behavior. This encourages the model to rely more on the external context for information.
 CONTROLS: Compare with the non-regularized version, and ablate different hyperparameters of the regularization term to understand its impact on performance.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Learning to Utilize External Context in RAG Systems
REVISED PROPOSAL: Extend the learned weighting scheme to incorporate not only the relevance of the retrieved documents to the question, but also their relevance to the generated response. This will enable the model to learn a better weighting scheme that takes into account the context in which the generated response is being produced, rather than just the question.
CONTROLS: Compare with the baseline uniform weighting scheme, the original learned weighting scheme that only incorporates query relevance, and ablate the additional response relevance component to understand its individual contribution.
COST: 10 GPU-hours, assuming 1000 queries and 10 retrieved documents each.
PREDICTION: This revised weighting scheme should show an improvement in hallucination detection rates and factual accuracy, particularly in tasks where the context in which the response is being produced is key to its correctness. However, there may be cases where the model overemphasizes the response relevance and ignores relevant documents that are not directly related to the response content.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Semantically-Aligned Multi-Layer Fusion for External Context
PROPOSAL: Design a multi-layer fusion mechanism that explicitly promotes the utilization of external context by aligning the semantic representations of the input query, the retrieved documents, and the external knowledge grounded in the documents. We will use a PSP (Pyramidal Simple Pyramid) module that maintains feature compatibility while still adapting external instruments concurrently at each level.
CONTROLS: Compare with a variant of proposal 1 that uses a simple averaging scheme for fusion, the non-fused model that doesn’t attempt to align these elements, and ablate the PSP module to understand its contribution to performance gains.
COST: 35 GPU-hours, assuming 1000 queries and 10 retrieved documents each.
PREDICTION: This mechanism should improve the model's ability to ground its responses in the external context, leading to a decrease in hallucination rates and an increase in factual accuracy. However, there may be performance degradation if the PSP module is not optimized correctly.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Hallucination Rates using a Contextualized Semantic Planner
PROPOSAL: Develop a contextualized semantic planner that integrates the model's internal and external knowledge to evaluate the plausibility and factuality of its responses. We will use a hierarchical planner that considers the context, question, and external knowledge to assess the model's hallucination rates.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline model that uses a standard evaluation metric (e.g., BLEU, ROUGE), and ablate different components of the planner to understand its impact on hallucination detection.
COST: 25 GPU-hours, assuming 1000 queries and 10 retrieved documents each.
PREDICTION: This planner should provide a more accurate and nuanced evaluation of the model's hallucination rates, leading to a better understanding of its strengths and weaknesses. However, there may be cases where the planner overemphasizes certain aspects of the context or knowledge, leading to biased evaluations.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Quantifying External Context Utilization via Contrastive Learning
REVISED PROPOSAL: Extend the contrastive learning objective to differentiate between hallucinations and factual responses. We will introduce a new positive class that represents factual responses, and encourage the model to learn representations that are maximally different between hallucinations and factual responses. This should lead to a more effective detection of hallucinations.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original contrastive learning objective, the baseline model that uses a standard supervised loss, and ablate different components of the revised objective to understand its impact on performance.
COST: 20 GPU-hours, assuming 1000 queries and 10 retrieved documents each.
PREDICTION: This revised objective should improve the model's ability to detect hallucinations, leading to a reduction in hallucination rates and an increase in factual accuracy. However, there may be cases where the model overemphasizes the contrastive signal, leading to biased representations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of External Knowledge Granularity
PROPOSAL: Explore the effect of the granularity of the external knowledge on hallucination rates and factual accuracy. We will compare models that receive either fine-grained or coarse-grained external knowledge, and analyze the impact of knowledge granularity on the model's performance.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline model that receives no external knowledge, and ablate different granularities of external knowledge to understand its impact on performance.
COST: 15 GPU-hours, assuming 1000 queries and 10 retrieved documents each.
PREDICTION: This study should provide insights into the optimal granularity of external knowledge that leads to improved hallucination detection and factual accuracy. However, there may be cases where the model overreliance on fine-grained knowledge leads to overfitting or underfitting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Ablating and Combining Approaches for Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: Perform an ablation study to investigate the contribution of each approach to hallucination detection, and combine the most effective approaches to create an ensemble model. We will also study the learning dynamics of the ensemble model to understand how it improves hallucination detection over time.
CONTROLS: Compare with the individual approaches and the baseline model, and analyze the performance of the ensemble model on different datasets and evaluation metrics.
COST: 40 GPU-hours, assuming 1000 queries and 10 retrieved documents each.
PREDICTION: This study should provide insights into the strengths and weaknesses of each approach and the ensemble model, leading to a deeper understanding of hallucination detection in RAG systems. However, there may be cases where the ensemble model overfitting or underfitting, especially if the individual approaches have conflicting strengths.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:Comparison of Language Modeling Distributions for Evaluating External Context Utilization
PROPOSAL: Analyze the similarity between the distribution of generated text and the distribution over relevant sentences in the retrieved documents using metrics such as Kullback-Leibler divergence, Jensen-Shannon divergence, and earth movers distance. Define a signal of external context utilization as the difference between these similarity metrics when generated text is compared to the retrieved documents vs. when it is compared to a placeholder or random text. Test this on three baselines: upper bounding RAG hans human performance, using RAG hans with an optimal retrieval strategy, and a T5-base model fine-tuned on a correction task.
CONTROLS: Upper bounding RAG hans human performance, T5-base fine-tuned on correction task, RAG hans with optimal retrieval strategy
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed signal should correlate well with the intended notion of external context utilization, and may be more effective than existing methods at detecting hallucinations in RAG systems, especially in retrieval-augmented question answering and news summarization tasks. However, may not generalize well to cases where the retrieved documents are very dissimilar from the actual information needed to complete the task.

Note: The choice on finite divergence metrics as opposed to similarities comes from separability discussion about "external content utilizations"

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:Context-Agnostic Signal for Internal Knowledge Utilization using Graph Attention Networks
PROPOSAL: Train a graph attention network (GAT) to encode the generated text and the internal model knowledge as nodes in a weighted graph, and propose a signal of internal knowledge utilization as the difference between the attention weights of the generated text node and the internal model knowledge node. Validate on three sociolinguistic and two text summarization datasets to test if this method is more resistant to domain adaptation challenges and captures the intended notion of internal knowledge utilization more accurately than existing methods.
CONTROLS: JSh, RD, TopN probe which only capture self-infposignature-value about token importance
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach may generalize well across models and domains and perform better than current metrics which require knowledge of specific model architecture.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISE Graph Attention Networks
PROPOSAL: REVISE 2. Context-Agnostic Signal for Internal Knowledge Utilization using Graph Attention Networks to train the GAT on the same document that contains the query or prompt, then compare the generated text node and internal model knowledge node weights within that subgraph to estimate the amount of internal knowledge utilized. This should capture a more accurate notion of internal knowledge utilization when the model draws from its pre-existing knowledge, even if that knowledge isn't necessarily relevant to the task at hand.
CONTROLS: JSh, RD, TopN probe which only capture self-infposignature-value about token importance
COST: 100 GPU-hours (reduced from 200)
PREDICTION: This subgraph-based method should lead to a more nuanced understanding of how internal knowledge influences generated text, and may help mitigate the over-reliance on internal knowledge that can lead to hallucinations in RAG systems.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Effectiveness of Knowledge Grounding as an Indicator of Hallucination
PROPOSAL: Develop a knowledge grounding method that evaluates whether the generated response is grounded in the retrieved documents by analyzing the alignment between the entities, events, and concepts in the generated text and the corresponding entities, events, and concepts in the retrieved documents. Use various alignment metrics (e.g., semantic similarity, entity overlap, dependency parsing) to calculate the knowledge grounding score, and evaluate its effectiveness in detecting hallucinations in RAG systems.
CONTROLS: signal of internal knowledge utilization, average retrieval quality
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method may provide an effective and model-agnostic way to detect hallucinations by assessing the alignment between the generated text and the supporting evidence from the retrieved documents, especially when combined with the first proposal on comparing language modeling distributions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Contextualized Retrieval-Augmented Generation Evaluation
PROPOSAL: Develop a contextualized evaluation framework that incorporates the external context (retrieved documents) and internal knowledge (generated text) in the evaluation process to detect hallucinations in RAG systems. Utilize attention mechanisms to align the input prompt, retrieved documents, and generated text, and compute the contextualized similarity score between the aligned prompt and generated text with the aligned retrieved documents. Validate the proposed framework on various real-world applications (e.g., news summarization, retrieval-augmented question answering).
CONTROLS: Knowledge grounding score, internal knowledge utilization signal
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This contextualized evaluation framework may provide more accurate and effective hallucination detection compared to state-of-the-art methods by capturing the complex interactions between the input context, retrieved documents, and generated text.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISE Contextualized Retrieval-Augmented Generation Evaluation
PROPOSAL: REVISE 4. Contextualized Retrieval-Augmented Generation Evaluation to use both qualitative and quantitative evaluation metrics. Use qualitative methods such as human annotators to label hallucinations and non-hallucinations in generated text and use quantitative metrics such as cross-entropy loss and BLEU score to evaluate the difference between generated text and retrieved documents. This will provide a more comprehensive evaluation of the proposed framework and its ability to detect hallucinations in RAG systems.
CONTROLS: Knowledge grounding score, internal knowledge utilization signal, human labels
COST: 30 more GPU-hours (350 total, including models baseline for cross-entropy and BLEU score computations)
PREDICTION: This revised framework should provide a more nuanced understanding of its effectiveness in detecting hallucinations and shed light on the relationships between different evaluation metrics and the proposed contextualized approach.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Zero-Shot Transfer of Internal Knowledge Utilization Signals
PROPOSAL: Train a signal adapter model that can transfer internal knowledge utilization signals from a source model to a target model in a zero-shot setting. The adapter model takes as input the input sequence, retrieved documents, and generated text of the source model, and predicts the internal knowledge utilization signal based on the knowledge learned from the source model. Evaluate the adapter model on various RAG models and show its ability to generalize the internal knowledge utilization signal across different models and domains.
CONTROLS: Average internal knowledge utilization signal, source and target model performance
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This signal adapter model may provide a way to generalize internal knowledge utilization signals across different models and domains, reducing the need for retraining the signal model for each new model or domain.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-Learning for Hallucination Detection in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
PROPOSAL: Use meta-learning to adapt the hallucination detection model to new RAG models, tasks, and domains. Train a meta-model that learns how to adapt a hallucination detection module to a new RAG model, and evaluate the performance on various target models and tasks. This can provide a way to efficiently adapt hallucination detection models to new models and tasks without retraining from scratch.
CONTROLS: Zero-shot transfer of internal knowledge utilization signals, meta-model generalization
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This meta-learning approach may provide a way to efficiently adapt hallucination detection models to new models and tasks, leading to improved performance and generalization across different RAG models and domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Identification of Hallucinations through Latent Contextual Analysis
PROPOSAL: Use Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) to model the latent space of the input context, and reconstruct the context given the generated text. Analyze the discrepancies between the input context and the reconstructed context to identify potential hallucinations. This method can provide insights into how the model deviates from the original input context and may lead to more accurate hallucination detection.
CONTROLS: Contextualized retrieval-augmented generation evaluation, knowledge grounding score
COST: 350 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This VAE-based approach may provide a novel way to identify hallucinations by analyzing the discrepancies between the input context and the reconstructed context, and may offer additional insights into the underlying mechanisms of hallucination.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards Unified Hallucination Detection in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
PROPOSAL: Integrate the previously proposed methods (1-7) to develop a unified hallucination detection framework for RAG systems. Evaluate the performance of the unified framework on a dataset of real-world RAG examples, assessing its ability to detect hallucinations effectively and efficiently.
CONTROLS: All previous proposals, unified framework performance
COST: < cumulative cost of all previous proposals > (approximately 2000-2500 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: This unified framework may provide a comprehensive hallucination detection solution for RAG systems, leveraging the strengths of each individual method to achieve improved performance and robustness across various applications and tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Joint Attention and Embedding Analysis for Hallucination Detection in RAG
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether a joint analysis of attention weights and contextual embeddings can detect hallucinations in RAG systems. Specifically, compute the similarity between generated text tokens and the retrieved context's embeddings using a measure like the Earth Mover's Distance (EMD), and combine this with attention weight-based metrics to obtain a holistic measure of external context utilization. 
CONTROLS: Use ReDeEP as a baseline to compare the effectiveness of the joint attention and embedding analysis.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might demonstrate improved generalizability and robustness over previous methods, but could fail if the EMD measure is not robust to changing base embedding spaces or fine-grained model specifics.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Robustness and Effectiveness Evaluation of Joint Attention and Embedding Analysis
PROPOSAL: Revise the joint attention and embedding analysis (Proposal 1) to include a robustness and effectiveness evaluation component. Investigate the effects of different retrieval algorithms, external knowledge source types, and hallucination types (e.g., factual vs. semantic hallucinations) on the approach's performance. Also, introduce additional controls, such as performance comparisons against retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems with and without filtered output and knowledge graph-based baselines.
CONTROLS: Compare to the filtered output and knowledge graph-based baselines, as well as to RAG systems generated using different retrieval algorithms and external knowledge sources.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised approach might demonstrate robustness to various retrieval algorithms and external knowledge source types, but could fail if the added controls introduce significant variability in results.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Robustness and Effectiveness Evaluation of Joint Attention and Embedding Analysis
PROPOSAL: Revise the joint attention and embedding analysis (Proposal 1) to include a robustness and effectiveness evaluation component. Investigate the effects of different retrieval algorithms, external knowledge source types, and hallucination types (e.g., factual vs. semantic hallucinations) on the approach's performance. Also, introduce additional controls, such as performance comparisons against retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems with and without filtered output and knowledge graph-based baselines.
CONTROLS: 
- Filtered output baseline: Compare to RAG systems where output is filtered using external knowledge sources.
- Knowledge graph-based baselines: Compare to RAG systems incorporating knowledge graphs for context.
- Retrieval Algorithms: Compare results from different retrieval algorithms (e.g., BM25, DPR, and Dense Passage Retriever).
- External Knowledge Sources: Compare results using different sources of external knowledge (e.g., Wikipedia, WebNLG, and BookCorpus).
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised approach might demonstrate robustness to various retrieval algorithms and external knowledge source types, but could fail if the added controls introduce significant variability in results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Bounds for External Context Utilization in RAG
PROPOSAL: Investigate theoretical bounds on the minimum external context utilization required for accurate response generation. Derive bounds based on the Shannon entropy of the external context and the generated response, assuming the retriever selects documents that maximize the mutual information between the context and the response. Analyze the implications of these bounds for the design of effective hallucination detection systems.
CONTROLS: Assume an ideal retriever that maximizes mutual information between context and response.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This theoretical analysis might provide insights on the fundamental limitations of external context utilization, but could fail if the assumption of an ideal retriever is too optimistic or limiting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Curriculum Learning for Improved External Context Utilization
PROPOSAL: Develop a curriculum learning framework to guide the retriever in selecting documents that maximize external context utilization. Design the curriculum to gradually increase the difficulty of the external context (e.g., longer documents, less relevant context), allowing the model to learn to effectively incorporate external knowledge into its responses.
CONTROLS: Compare to a non-curriculum learning approach and evaluate the impact of the difficulty progression on the model's performance.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might demonstrate improved external context utilization, but could fail if the curriculum is not properly designed, leading to inconsistent or decreased performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Quality of Retrieved Documents for Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of document quality on hallucination detection in RAG systems. Develop metrics to assess the quality of retrieved documents, such as relevance, coherence, and factual accuracy. Analyze how these metrics affect the performance of existing hallucination detection methods and explore the potential benefits of using a document quality-aware approach.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of hallucination detection methods on high-quality vs. low-quality retrieved documents.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might demonstrate improved hallucination detection performance when using high-quality documents, but could fail if the document quality metrics are not effective in capturing the relevant features.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Using Knowledge Graph Embeddings for Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of knowledge graph embeddings (KGEs) to augment the external context for hallucination detection. Represent entities and relations in the knowledge graph as embeddings and incorporate these embeddings into the retrieval process. Evaluate the performance of the approach on different types of hallucinations.
CONTROLS: Compare to a baseline that uses only the text retriever and to a variant that uses a combination of text and KGE retrievers.
COST: 2500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might demonstrate improved hallucination detection performance, especially for queries that require rich entity and relation information, but could fail if the KGEs do not capture the relevant relations correctly.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Explainable Retrieval for Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of explainable retrieval methods to provide insights into the retrieval process and improve hallucination detection. Evaluate the performance of different explainable retrieval methods, such as SALSA and OptUN , and their ability to identify relevant documents and entities for hallucination detection.
CONTROLS: Compare to a non-explainable retrieval approach and evaluate the impact of different explainable retrieval methods on hallucination detection performance.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might demonstrate improved explainability and potentially improved hallucination detection performance, but could fail if the explainable retrieval methods are not effective in identifying the relevant documents and entities.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Improved External Context Utilization in RAG
PROPOSAL: Revisit the joint attention and embedding analysis (Proposal 1) and explore the use of transfer learning to leverage knowledge from pre-trained language models and external context for improved hallucination detection. Investigate the impact of fine-tuning the pre-trained models on the external context and its influence on hallucination detection performance.
CONTROLS: Compare to a non-transfer learning approach and evaluate the performance on different types of hallucinations.
COST: 2200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised approach might demonstrate improved hallucination detection performance by leveraging the knowledge from pre-trained language models and external context, but could fail if the transfer learning process is not effective in capturing the relevant features.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Learning for Simultaneous Hallucination Detection and Knowledge Retrieval
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of multi-task learning to improve hallucination detection and retrieve relevant information simultaneously. Train a model to learn both hallucination detection and knowledge retrieval tasks in a shared input space. Evaluate the performance of the approach on hallucination detection and knowledge retrieval and investigate its effectiveness in real-world scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare to a single-task learning approach and evaluate the performance on different types of hallucinations.
COST: 3500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might demonstrate improved performance on both hallucination detection and knowledge retrieval, but could fail if the shared input space is not effective in capturing the relevant features for both tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Grounded Retrieval Augmentation (GRA) for Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: We implement a grounded retrieval augmentation (GRA) system to quantify the utilization of external context and internal knowledge in RAG systems. GRA supplements traditional RAG with an additional decoder that takes the retrieved documents and internal knowledge as input and produces an augmented representation. We use a pre-trained contrastive language model (CLM) to calculate the similarity between the augmented representation and the retrieved documents, and compare it with the similarity between the generated text and the retrieved documents. GRA aims to provide a more accurate measure of external context utilization.
CONTROLS: A baseline RAG system with traditional retrieval augmentation and ablation study to remove the additional decoder and analyze the effect of the augmented representation.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect GRA to significantly improve hallucination detection performance, especially in scenarios where the retrieved documents are sufficient to answer the question, by avoiding over-reliance on internal knowledge. However, the additional decoder may increase computational cost and require more training data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Alignment Regularization for Improved Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: Inspired by recent work on alignment between encoder and decoder representations in transformers, we propose alignment regularization to reinforce the RAG system to strongly adhere to the retrieved documents. We add a regularization term to the loss function that encourages the model to generate text that is aligned with the retrieved documents, both syntactically and semantically. This regularization term promotes the utilization of the external context, making it more difficult for the model to hallucinate.
CONTROLS: Investigating GRA (proposed in turn 1) with and without alignment regularization to evaluate the additional benefit of alignment regularization.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect alignment regularization to further improve hallucination detection performance by encouraging the RAG system to utilize the external context more effectively. However, this regularization term may require careful tuning, and in some cases, over-regularization might occur, leading to degradation in model performance.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating Grounded Retrieval Augmentation (GRA) for Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: We modify the GRA system proposed in turn 1 to include the alignment regularization technique introduced in turn 2. The additional decoder is designed to not only produce an augmented representation but also to align it with the retrieved documents through the alignment regularization term. This modification aims to leverage the benefits of both GRA and alignment regularization for improved hallucination detection.
CONTROLS: A baseline RAG system with traditional retrieval augmentation, GRA without alignment regularization, and alignment regularization without GRA to analyze the impact of each individual component and their combination.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (up from 100, due to the increased complexity of the combined model)
PREDICTION: By combining GRA and alignment regularization, we expect to see a more significant improvement in hallucination detection performance, as the model is now encouraged to utilize both the internal knowledge and the external context effectively. However, the increased complexity of the combined model may lead to overfitting or require more careful tuning of hyperparameters.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Alignment Regularization for Improved Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: To further analyze the impact of alignment regularization, we propose an experiment to evaluate its effectiveness on different attention mechanisms in the RAG system. We investigate the impact of attention mechanisms such as BERT-attention, Transformers' multi-head attention, and locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) on the performance of alignment regularization. This experiment aims to understand whether alignment regularization has a universal benefit across different attention mechanisms or if it is sensitive to the specific attention mechanism used.
CONTROLS: Baseline RAG system with traditional retrieval augmentation and alignment regularization applied to each attention mechanism individually to evaluate their impact.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect alignment regularization to have a positive impact on hallucination detection performance across different attention mechanisms, although the magnitude of the improvement may vary depending on the specific attention mechanism used.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Augmentation-Based External Context Embeddings for Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: Inspired by the success of data augmentation in NLP, we propose a novel approach to enhance the RAG system by designing augmentation-based external context embeddings. Specifically, we create multiple versions of the retrieved documents by applying random transformations such as paraphrasing, fluency editing, or content expansion. These augmented document versions are then embedded into the input representation of the RAG system, allowing the model to consider multiple perspectives of the external context. Our hypothesis is that this augmentation-based approach will lead to improved hallucination detection performance by encouraging the model to utilize the external context more robustly.
CONTROLS: Baseline RAG system with traditional retrieval augmentation and a simple variant of the proposed approach that uses a fixed set of transformations instead of random ones.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect augmentation-based external context embeddings to significantly improve hallucination detection performance by forcing the model to be more robust and context-sensitive. However, the choice of transformations and the extent of augmentation may require careful tuning, and excessive augmentation could lead to overfitting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing the Role of Retrieval Representations in Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: Our goal is to investigate the relationship between the quality of retrieval representations and hallucination detection performance. We propose to modify the RAG system to output multiple retrieval representations, each representing a different aspect of the external context. We then examine the impact of the choice of representation on hallucination detection performance. Our hypothesis is that selecting an optimal representation will enable the model to more effectively utilize the external context, leading to improved hallucination detection performance.
CONTROLS: Baseline RAG system using a single retrieval representation and an experiment where retrieval representations are generated using different types of encoders (e.g., BERT, RoBERTa, etc.).
COST: 70 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the choice of retrieval representation to have a significant impact on hallucination detection performance, and selecting an optimal representation will lead to improved results. However, the optimal representation may vary depending on the specific characteristics of the task and the data, and selecting the best representation could be challenging.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Alignment Regularization for Improved Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: To refine the alignment regularization approach, we propose to incorporate graph-based attention into the RAG system. Specifically, we design a graph where nodes represent tokens from the generated text and the external context, and edges represent the attention weights between them. The alignment regularization term is then applied to the node embeddings and edge weights to promote the alignment between the generated text and the external context. Our hypothesis is that graph-based attention will enable the model to capture more nuanced relationships between tokens and improve hallucination detection performance.
CONTROLS: Experiment comparing the original alignment regularization approach with the graph-based alignment regularization variant, as well as a baseline RAG system without any alignment regularization.
COST: 40 GPU-hours (additional to the original 50 GPU-hours, due to the additional complexity of graph-based attention)
